newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS-Russian markets shrug off Yeltsin news, stable.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Russian markets shrug off Yeltsin news, stable.

text.p: Russian markets on Friday shrugged off fears set off by President Boris Yeltsin's announcement that he would have a heart operation, and recovered some early losses, but many traders said a prolonged rise was unlikely.
Most markets fell in the first half hour of trade on Friday, prolonging the panic late on Thursday when Yeltsin announced he would undergo heart surgery in Russia at the end of the month.

The stock market, where bid prices on leading shares fell up to 10 percent in 45 minutes of trade on Thursday, turned around after an hour of trade, and rose during the day after some investors rushed in to snap up cheap stock, traders said.

"Local traders made a bet that the West was going to sell with a vengeance and that didn't happen. Now they are trying to stem their losses," said Troika-Dialog bank senior equities salesman Terry Olin.
Utility Mosenergo traded at $0.964 after a morning low of about $0.925 and Thursday's close of $0.960. It had been trading at about one dollar before Yeltsin's announcement.

"There are still some dramatic spreads, but they are narrowing -- they are nothing like yesterday's levels," when the gap between bid and ask prices doubled for some issues after Yeltsin's news, Olin said.

Interfax news agency quoted a senior doctor on Friday as saying Yeltsin would have bypass surgery -- a relatively common procedure. Some traders had worried that Yeltsin's condition required more complicated treatment.

But some traders said the operation would stifle the spectacular growth expected by many traders for later this year, since major Western investors would hold off investment, waiting to see how Yeltsin recovers from the operation.

"The upside potential is much lower in the next few months than the downside," said Alfa-Capital chief equities trader Alexander Bubnovski. "In the next few months it will be difficult to make 100 percent profit."

Some dealers expected share price drops of 10 percent or more by the end of the month and a freeze in trading similar to that after Yeltsin's election run-off victory July 3, when prices plummeted and a nervous market sat on its hands rather than trade.
The domestic treasury bill (GKO) and dollar-denominated MinFin bond markets also rebounded from initial drops on Friday, and short-term domestic paper closed slightly higher.

The yield on the six-month GKO maturing in early January 1997 (series number 22038) fell to 53.93 from 56.67 percent on Thursday, but the yield on the six-month bill issued this week and maturing in April 1997 (series number 22048) rose to 77.17 from 76.45 percent.
Alliance-Menatep trader Dmitry Falkovich said prices could fall at the end of the month when the operation is closer to hand, but in the mean time fundamentals would rule the game.
"The market has been very stable, thanks to the Central Bank and its affiliates. The question is how much the central bank will support (the market)," he said.
Budget deficit problems and unresolved issues of foreigner participation were still important factors, he added.
MinFins also settled back after a little early action. "Prices rose in the beginning some 0.3-0.4 points but then fell back to earlier levels," said Avtobank dealer Alla Zakharova.

The rouble eased slightly during morning trade, falling to 5,366 to the dollar from 5,363 at Thursday's close on the Moscow Interbank Currency Exchange (MICEX), but dealers said the minor move was not affected by Yeltsin's announcement.
Optimistic equities dealers said the market should have already factored in Yeltsin's health problems, though they said bad news could still destroy recent gains.

"This is plainly not fresh new information," said Olin. "The fact that Yeltsin is doing something about (his heart condition) that millions of people have done successflly should not remove resason for investing in this market."
